notes.text: Radboud Molecular Life Sciences integrates molecular biology with sustained organic, inorganic, analytical and physical chemistry, synthesis and several specialist laboratories. UCR can study molecular, cellular, biomedical and neurobiological questions through biology, biochemistry, data and one broad life-science laboratory, but these programmes are related-fields responses rather than reproductions of the full molecular-science curriculum.

audience.programmeDescription: Molecular Life Sciences at Radboud combines molecular biology and medical science with a substantial foundation in chemistry, physics and mathematics. Students study molecular processes in health and disease through theory, computational work and laboratory research.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR programme develops molecular and cellular biology, biochemistry, genetics, immunity, pharmacology and disease mechanisms, supported by laboratory work and quantitative methods. It offers a related biomedical route. It does not reproduce Radboud’s organic, inorganic, analytical and physical chemistry, synthesis, spectroscopy, crystallography, specialist laboratory sequence or required research internship.

curriculum.routeLabel: Ordinary Molecular Life Sciences route; one permitted 18 EC elective selection
curriculum.limitation: The 180 EC framework consists of 105 EC required courses, 57 EC restricted differentiation study, a 12 EC research internship and 6 EC open electives. The three displayed 6 EC ML1 courses illustrate the required 18 EC selection. The other 39 EC must meet programme rules and is not unrestricted free choice. Academic skills, language assessment and writing requirements are integrated as specified; the first-year skills component and language assessment add no credits.

componentNotes.later-required-03: The first-year skills component carries no credits and includes writing assignments, a progress test, reflection and mandatory mentor activities. Final skills credits require portfolio completion, mentor meetings and twelve documented colloquia or similar activities across years two and three.
